results.key_finding: Incomplete (open) ring enhancement was far more frequent in demyelinating lesions than in tumours or abscesses, which usually enhance as a closed ring.
results.title: Open-ring imaging sign: highly specific for atypical brain demyelination (Masdeu JC et al.)

results.key_finding: In biopsy-proven tumefactive demyelination, mass effect and oedema were often modest for lesion size, ring enhancement was frequently incomplete, and most patients went on to a relapsing course.
results.title: Clinical and radiographic spectrum of pathologically confirmed tumefactive multiple sclerosis (Lucchinetti CF et al.)

results.key_finding: Supportive features include open-ring enhancement, peripheral restricted diffusion, intralesional veins, additional typical lesions and CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands; biopsy is reserved for cases in which imaging and CSF leave lymphoma or glioma in doubt or the course is atypical. Corticosteroids before biopsy can make lymphoma non-diagnostic.
results.title: Tumefactive demyelination: an approach to diagnosis and management (Hardy TA, Chataway J)

output.summary: Tumefactive demyelinating lesions can mimic neoplasm. Open-ring enhancement, modest mass effect, peripheral restricted diffusion, intralesional veins, additional typical lesions and CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands favour demyelination; biopsy is reserved for atypical or doubtful cases, and corticosteroids can obscure lymphoma.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not start corticosteroids before CSF cytology and flow cytometry are obtained: steroids can make lymphoma non-diagnostic
Do not resect the lesion or start oncological treatment (radiotherapy, chemotherapy) on the imaging appearance alone
Do not start teriflunomide in a woman of child-bearing potential without effective contraception (teratogenic, long elimination half-life)
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS: cord lesions count toward DIS and separate MS from NMOSD
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria, naming the regions that give DIS and, where needed, what gives DIT or positive CSF (here periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal cord, with the dominant lesion a tumefactive demyelinating lesion).

Treat the symptomatic tumefactive lesion (headache and vomiting with perilesional oedema) with IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3-5 days once CSF cytology and flow cytometry are negative, with a proton pump inhibitor while she takes ibuprofen and glucose monitoring.
Repeat gadolinium MRI in about 4-6 weeks to confirm regression of the tumefactive lesion, and proceed to stereotactic biopsy if it enlarges, fails to regress or develops atypical features.
Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (an enhancing tumefactive lesion with four-region disease), after discussing pregnancy plans and contraception.

Before starting disease-modifying therapy, screen HBsAg, anti-HBc, HCV, HIV (done) and VZV IgG, add anti-JCV antibodies if natalizumab is considered, and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before starting.

differential.key_features: Raised by a periventricular enhancing lesion; against it: open rather than homogeneous enhancement, peripheral rather than whole-lesion restricted diffusion, no lipid peak on spectroscopy, CSF cytology and flow cytometry negative, HIV negative, and four-region disease with a cord lesion. Not excluded by tissue.
Open ring toward the cortex, mild mass effect for size, Cho/NAA 0.9 without a lipid peak, multiple other typical lesions and CSF-restricted bands argue against it.
Normal CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis; open rather than closed ring; additional ovoid white matter and cord lesions.
Afebrile with normal CRP and ESR; peripheral rather than central restricted diffusion; tuberculin skin test negative; CSF AFB smear negative and CSF culture sterile.
AQP4-IgG negative by cell-based assay; short dorsal C2-C3 lesion rather than longitudinally extensive myelitis; no optic neuritis or area postrema syndrome; CSF-restricted bands.
MOG-IgG negative by cell-based assay; no optic neuritis, ADEM-like or conus lesions; CSF-restricted bands, uncommon in MOGAD.
No encephalopathy, no preceding infection or vaccination, a 7-month course and ovoid lesions with enhancing and non-enhancing components.
Serum ACE 28 U/L and calcium normal, no leptomeningeal enhancement, no hilar adenopathy on CT.
ANA and anti-dsDNA negative; no systemic features.

key_clinical_evidence: Five months of Lhermitte sign with brisk patellar reflexes and bilateral extensor plantars, explained by a dorsal C2-C3 cord lesion; seven months of progressive headache with vomiting and a dominant 2.1 cm right periventricular enhancing lesion with mild oedema.

DIS: 4 of 5 regions: periventricular (right 2.1 cm lesion, left frontal horn lesion), juxtacortical (left parietal), infratentorial (left middle cerebellar peduncle), spinal cord (C2-C3). Four regions establish DIS without a separate DIT; the scan also shows an enhancing lesion with non-enhancing lesions.

Tumefactive features favouring demyelination: open ring enhancement with the open side toward the cortex, peripheral restricted diffusion, intralesional venules on SWI, mild oedema without midline shift, and spectroscopy with Cho/NAA 0.9 and no lipid peak.
Positive CSF: five CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands and kFLC index 42.0 (reference < 6.1); 2 cells/uL with negative cytology and flow cytometry.
AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG negative by cell-based assay, normal CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, afebrile with normal CRP: against NMOSD, MOGAD, metastasis and abscess.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: a dominant 2.1 cm enhancing lesion with oedema in a woman referred for a suspected brain mass. The clues to tumefactive demyelination (open-ring enhancement toward the cortex, intralesional venules, peripheral restricted diffusion, satellite lesions in typical regions, a C2-C3 cord lesion explaining the Lhermitte sign, CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands) must be combined before biopsy or oncological treatment is considered.

patient.history_present_illness: A 37-year-old right-handed Saudi female elementary school teacher with no significant prior medical history presents for inpatient evaluation after being referred by her primary care physician for a suspected intracranial mass lesion. She reports a progressive frontal headache that began approximately 7 months ago, initially intermittent and mild but gradually worsening over the past 3 months to become near-constant and moderate in severity. The headache is described as a bilateral frontal pressure sensation, distinct from her previous occasional tension headaches, and is not associated with photophobia, phonophobia, visual aura, or postural changes. She has experienced frequent nausea and vomiting over the past 2-3 months, occurring approximately 3-4 times per week, occasionally triggered by bending forward or straining. Approximately 5 months ago, she began experiencing brief episodes of electric shock-like sensations radiating from her neck down into all four limbs, lasting only 1-2 seconds and occurring multiple times daily, particularly when she looks down at her desk while teaching. She denies any focal weakness, persistent numbness or tingling, visual changes, diplopia, hearing loss, difficulty swallowing, sphincter dysfunction, urinary incontinence, or bowel changes. She has not experienced any seizures. She reports mild fatigue over the past 3 months and has noticed some difficulty concentrating at work, which she attributes to the persistent headache and poor sleep from nausea. There has been no weight loss, night sweats, fever, rash, joint pain, or other systemic symptoms. She was previously started on sumatriptan and ibuprofen by her primary care physician for a presumed migraine diagnosis approximately 4 months ago, but has had no significant improvement. Her physician subsequently ordered outpatient imaging which raised concern for a possible brain lesion, prompting this referral for further evaluation.
